      <content name="title"><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span></content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0">Generalized</span> <span class="qt1">Anxiety</span> Disorder</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>?<p><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span> is a feeling of fear, dread, and uneasiness. It might cause you to sweat, feel restless and <span class="qt1">tense</span>, and have a rapid heartbeat.   It can be a normal reaction to <span class="qt1">stress</span>. For example, you might feel <span class="qt1">anxious</span> when faced with a difficult problem at work, before taking a test, or before making an important decision. It can help you to cope. The <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> may give you a boost of energy or help you focus. But for people with <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders, the fear is not temporary and can be overwhelming.</p>What are <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p><span class="qt1">Anxiety</span> disorders are conditions in which you have <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> that does not go away and can get worse over time. The symptoms can interfere with daily activities such as job performance, schoolwork, and relationships.</p>What are the types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p>There are several types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders, including: </p><ul><li><span class="qt0">Generalized</span> <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorder (GAD). People with GAD worry about ordinary issues such as health, money, work, and family. But their worries are excessive, and they have them almost every day for at least 6 months.</li><li>Panic disorder. People with panic disorder have panic attacks. These are sudden, repeated periods of intense fear when there is no danger. The attacks come on quickly and can last several minutes or more.</li><li>Phobias. People with phobias have an intense fear of something that poses little or no actual danger. Their fear may be about spiders, flying, going to crowded places, or being in social situations (known as social <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>).</li></ul>What causes <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p>The cause of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> is unknown. Factors such as genetics, brain biology and chemistry, <span class="qt1">stress</span>, and your environment may play a role.</p>Who is at risk for <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p>The risk factors for the different types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders can vary. For example, GAD and phobias are more common in women, but social <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> affects men and women equally. There are some general risk factors for all types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders, including:</p><ul><li>Certain personality traits, such as being shy or withdrawn when you are in new situations or meeting new people</li><li>Traumatic events in early childhood or adulthood</li><li>Family history of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> or other mental disorders</li><li>Some physical health conditions, such as thyroid problems or arrhythmia</li></ul>What are the symptoms of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p>The different types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders can have different symptoms. But they all have a combination of:</p><ul><li><span class="qt1">Anxious</span> thoughts or beliefs that are hard to control. They make you feel restless and <span class="qt1">tense</span> and interfere with your daily life. They do not go away and can get worse over time.</li><li>Physical symptoms, such as a pounding or rapid heartbeat, unexplained aches and pains, dizziness, and shortness of breath</li><li>Changes in behavior, such as avoiding everyday activities you used to do</li></ul><p>Using caffeine, other substances, and certain medicines can make your symptoms worse.</p>How are <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders diagnosed?<p>To diagnose <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders, your health care provider will ask about your symptoms and medical history. You may also have a physical exam and lab tests to make sure that a different health problem is not the cause of your symptoms.</p><p>If you don't have another health problem, you will get a psychological evaluation. Your provider may do it, or you may be referred to a mental health professional to get one.</p>What are the treatments for <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders?<p>The main treatments for <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders are psychotherapy (talk therapy), medicines, or both:</p><ul><li>Psychotherapy can help you recognize and change troubling emotions, thoughts, and behaviors. To be effective, it should focus on your specific <span class="qt1">anxieties</span> and needs. There are many types; some of the types used for <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders include:
  <ul><li>Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), which teaches you different ways of thinking and behaving. It can help you change how you react to the things that cause you to feel fear and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>. It may include exposure therapy. This therapy focuses on having you confront your fears so that you will be able to do the things that you had been avoiding.</li><li>Acceptance and commitment therapy may help with some <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders. It uses strategies such as mindfulness and goal setting to reduce discomfort and <span class="qt1">anxiety</span>.</li></ul> 
</li><li>Medicines to treat <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders include anti-<span class="qt1">anxiety</span> medicines and certain antidepressants. Some types of medicines may work better for specific types of <span class="qt1">anxiety</span> disorders. You should work closely with your provider to identify which medicine is best for you. You may need to try more than one medicine before you can find the right one.</li></ul><p>Support groups and <span class="qt1">stress</span> management techniques may also be helpful.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>

      <content name="title">Child Mental Health</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Mental Health, Child</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>It's important to recognize and treat mental illnesses in children early on.  Once mental illness develops, it becomes a regular part of your child's behavior. This makes it more difficult to treat.</p><p>But it's not always easy to know when your child has a serious problem. Everyday stresses can cause changes in your child's behavior. For example, getting a new brother or sister or going to a new school may cause a child to temporarily act out. Warning signs that it might be a more serious problem include:</p><ul><li>Problems in more than one setting (at school, at home, with peers)</li><li>Changes in appetite or sleep</li><li>Social withdrawal or fear of things he or she did not used to be not afraid of</li><li>Returning to behaviors more common in younger children, such as bedwetting</li><li>Signs of being upset, such as sadness or tearfulness</li><li>Signs of self-destructive behavior, such as head-banging or suddenly getting hurt often</li><li>Repeated thoughts of death</li></ul><p>To diagnose mental health problems, the doctor or mental health specialist looks at your child's signs and symptoms, medical history, and family history. Treatments include medicines and talk therapy.</p><p>NIH: National Institute of Mental Health</p></content>
